paper_metadata.title: Preparing Arbitrary Continuous Functions in Quantum Registers With Logarithmic Complexity

summary: The paper proposes a gate‑based algorithm for preparing quantum states encoding arbitrary continuous functions using adiabatic evolution under a rank‑1 Hamiltonian. The authors prove query complexity O(F^p / ε^2) (p = −4 for pointwise encoding) independent of qubit count n, and numerically simulate state preparation for up to n = 12 qubits (2n‑qubit simulation) showing infidelity decreasing roughly as O(r^-1.2) with iteration count r and reaching ~10^-6–10^-3.

experiments.description: Direct state preparation of discretized continuous functions via adiabatic evolution under a rank-1 Hamiltonian, demonstrated numerically on a log-normal distribution and a Slater-type function.

algorithm.variant: adiabatic state preparation using rank-1 Hamiltonian simulation

hyperparameters.evolution_time_T: constant-bounded; selected to satisfy adiabatic condition
hyperparameters.function_discretization_bits_d: used in oracle encoding; 32 bits in numerical simulations

algorithm.parameter_initialization: initial state |+>^n; interpolated from trivial function f0 to target function f1

problem_formulation.encoding_details: n-qubit register encodes samples f(x_j) on a uniform grid; amplitudes proportional to function values
problem_formulation.objective_function: prepare |psi> = (1/N) sum_j f(x_j)|j> for a discretized continuous function f
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: adiabatic interpolation between easy-to-prepare f0 and target f1; no explicit penalty terms
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: H(s) = -A(s)/N, where A(s) is rank-1 with entries [A(s)]_kl = f_s(x_k) f_s^*(x_l)
problem_formulation.num_ancilla_qubits: n + d + 2 ancillary qubits in the low-rank simulation subroutine

problem_instance.description: Preparation of continuous functions on [a,b], with numerical examples for a log-normal distribution and a Slater-type orbital

dataset_specification.description: log-normal distribution and Slater-type function defined analytically; no external dataset

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: uniform discretization of the interval into N=2^n grid points; function values encoded with d-bit precision; in simulations d=32
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: theoretical analysis plus numerical simulations of state-preparation infidelity versus qubit count n and iteration count r

hardware.framework: custom classical numerical simulation of the algorithm (exact simulation of the 1‑sparse dynamics)

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: function evaluation via arithmetic/oracle; numerical digitization of function values to d bits
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: measure ancilla and discard/reset; compute state-preparation infidelity from simulated overlaps

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: infidelity decreases approximately polynomially with r; empirical scaling around O(r^-1.19) to O(r^-1.3) in simulations

speedup_claims.factor: logarithmic complexity in resolution / exponential quantum advantage
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical state preparation / direct evaluation over all grid points
speedup_claims.conditions: fault-tolerant gate-based quantum computer; efficiently computable function; favorable filling ratio; asymptotic regime
speedup_claims.caveats: Complexity depends on filling ratio F; pathological narrow-peak functions can remove the advantage; paper’s numerical results are simulations, not hardware demonstrations.

speedup_claims.factor: constant query complexity in number of qubits
speedup_claims.conditions: asymptotically in n for continuous functions
speedup_claims.caveats: Constant refers to oracle-query complexity; total cost still depends on function evaluation and filling ratio.

speedup_claims.factor: exponential speedup for sampling from probability densities
speedup_claims.conditions: when using the prepared state and measuring it; assuming efficient state preparation
speedup_claims.caveats: Claimed in discussion; not benchmarked against a classical sampler in the paper.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(F^p / epsilon^2) query complexity for state preparation, with p = -4 for pointwise encoding and p = -2 for integral encoding; overall O(r) in the number of adiabatic/simulation steps
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical direct search for pathological narrow-peak instances is O(2^(2n)) in the paper's counterexample; for generic function loading no classical benchmark is characterized

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not determined; complexity expressed asymptotically in filling ratio F and precision ε but no concrete classical runtime comparison or crossover N* given.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires fault‑tolerant quantum computer capable of implementing repeated Hamiltonian simulation steps and oracle evaluation for f(x) with poly(n,d) arithmetic; algorithm assumes efficient oracle/QRAM access to function values.
limiting_factors: No hardware experiments; only noiseless classical simulation
Algorithm relies on fault‑tolerant Hamiltonian simulation and arithmetic oracles
Performance depends strongly on filling ratio F, which can be exponentially small for pathological cases
Efficient oracle or QRAM for function evaluation is assumed but not demonstrated
No empirical comparison against classical implementations

notes: hardware.type inferred as simulator_other because the paper reports explicit numerical simulations of the algorithm and does not name a physical QPU.
num_qubits reported from the text: the implementation uses two n-qubit registers plus d and 2 ancillas; simulations explicitly mention 2n-qubit exact 1-sparse simulation and d=32.
circuit_depth reported only asymptotically as O(r) / O(d) per step; no transpiled depth or gate counts are given.
